content.title: About
content.content: Dried apricots are the fruit of the apricot tree (Prunus armeniaca) that have been dehydrated to reduce moisture. They have a sweet‑tart flavor and a soft, slightly chewy texture. Dried apricots are widely used in cooking, baking, muesli, and as a convenient snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dried apricots are rich in beta‑carotene, a precursor of vitamin A.
In ancient cultures the apricot symbolized longevity and abundance.
They are a staple ingredient in many Mediterranean and Middle Eastern dishes.
When properly stored, dried apricots can keep for up to a year.
Apricots belong to the Rosaceae family and are closely related to peaches and plums.

items.title: High in vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene in apricots converts to vitamin A, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart health.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Iron is essential for hemoglobin formation and oxygen transport.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phenolic compounds protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Dried apricots have a high natural sugar level, so they should be eaten in moderation, especially by people with diabetes.

items.title: Sulfites
items.content: Sulfites are sometimes added to extend shelf life and may cause allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Food allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to apricots.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The natural acidity can irritate the stomach lining if consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dried apricots can be enjoyed as a snack, added to muesli, yogurt, baked goods, salads, or used to make compotes and sauces. Soaking them in water rehydrates the fruit and softens the texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried apricots in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer storage keep them in the refrigerator. Discard any apricots that show mold, off‑odors, or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Barbecue sauce is a thick, flavorful sauce made from tomatoes, vinegar, sugar, and spices, used for marinating, glazing, and serving with meat dishes, especially grilled and smoked foods. It has a sweet‑tart taste with a hint of smokiness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial barbecue sauce appeared in the United States in the early 1920s.
Traditional recipes include tomato paste, brown sugar, vinegar, mustard, and aromatic spices such as paprika, garlic, and onion powder.
Different U.S. regions have their own styles: Kentucky sauces are more tomato‑based, while Texas versions are spicier and smokier.
Barbecue sauce is often used both as a marinade and as a finishing glaze to create a caramelized crust.
Gluten‑free and vegan versions exist, substituting honey with maple syrup or agave.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and spices provide lycopene and polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Vinegar stimulates stomach acid production, aiding protein digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many sauces, barbecue sauce typically contains little fat when no oil is added.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: The tomato base supplies a modest amount of vitamin C, supporting the immune system.

items.title: Moderate sugar content
items.content: Sugar gives quick energy, but most commercial sauces have less sugar than sweet ketchup.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Some varieties contain a lot of added sugar, which can be problematic for diabetics or those watching weight.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Vinegar and salt make the sauce fairly salty; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Ingredients may include mustard, soy sauce, or dairy, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Commercial sauces often contain preservatives (e.g., sodium benzoate) that some sensitive individuals prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Use barbecue sauce as a marinade for chicken, pork, or beef, as a glaze during the last minutes of grilling, and as a dip for fries, veggie sticks, and burgers. It can also be mixed into salad dressings or incorporated into sauces for barbecue‑style dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the sauce in a tightly sealed jar in the refrigerator after opening. Unopened, it can be kept at room temperature for up to 12 months; once opened, use within 3‑4 weeks. Discard if mold, off‑color, or off‑smell appear.

chicken-leg-drumstick-and-thigh-stewed-s.title: Chicken leg, drumstick and thigh, stewed, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed chicken leg, drumstick and thigh without skin is a lean source of protein obtained by slow cooking in liquid. The method keeps the meat moist while the lack of skin reduces saturated fat content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken drumsticks and thighs contain more iron than breast meat.
Stewing preserves more B‑vitamins compared with frying.
Stewed chicken parts are staples in many Eastern European and Asian cuisines.
Cooking without skin dramatically lowers the cholesterol level of the dish.
Skin‑less chicken is easier to digest for people with sensitive stomachs.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 20 g of complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support normal blood formation and immune function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Stewed chicken is rich in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Removing the skin cuts saturated fat, making it heart‑friendly.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: Protein combined with a modest amount of fat helps you feel full longer.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Chicken must be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 74 °C; undercooking can lead to salmonella.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Added salt or ready‑made sauces can raise sodium levels, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Histamine formation
items.content: If stored too long, stewed meat can accumulate histamine, causing food intolerance.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Stewed legs, drumsticks and thighs can be served as a main dish, added to soups, stews, salads, or used as a filling for pies. Any remaining small bits of fat can be trimmed before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags for up to 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 74 °C before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Steamed salmon is a tender piece of fish cooked by steaming without added fats. This method preserves most nutrients while keeping the flavor mild and slightly sweet. Salmon is considered one of the healthiest seafoods thanks to its high omega‑3 fatty acids, protein, and vitamin content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Salmon can migrate over 3,000 km from the ocean to freshwater rivers to spawn.
In the wild, salmon change skin color with the season and breeding stage.
Steaming retains up to 90 % of vitamin D, which is important for bones and immunity.
Salmon is one of the few fish that contain significant amounts of astaxanthin, giving the flesh its pink hue.
In Japan, steamed salmon is often served with soy sauce and fresh ginger.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Omega‑3s support heart health, reduce inflammation, and promote brain function.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Salmon provides a complete set of essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D helps maintain strong bones, a robust immune system, and mood regulation.

items.title: Contains selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as a powerful antioxidant protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Steaming requires no added oil, keeping the dish light and heart‑friendly.

items.title: Risk of heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Some salmon may contain mercury or other toxins; choose reputable sources.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to seafood may experience reactions ranging from mild to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Spoilage if not stored properly
items.content: Fresh fillets deteriorate quickly; keep them at 0 °C or lower and use within 1–2 days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve steamed salmon hot, often with lemon, fresh dill, or soy sauce. It can be added to salads, rice dishes, or used as a filling for sushi rolls. For extra flavor, lightly season with salt and pepper before steaming.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh salmon in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0–2 °C and cook within 24–48 hours. Frozen salmon should be kept at –18 °C for up to 3 months; thaw it in the refrigerator before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Frozen garlic bread is a ready‑to‑bake product that includes a flavorful garlic butter spread, herbs, and cheese. After thawing and baking, it develops a crisp crust and a soft, aromatic interior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Garlic bread is a classic starter in Italian restaurants, often served alongside pasta.
Freezing preserves the fresh garlic aroma for several months without loss of flavor.
Traditional recipes add olive oil, Parmesan, and fresh herbs such as parsley or basil.
In many countries garlic bread is a popular street‑food snack.

items.title: Rich in garlic compounds
items.content: Garlic contains sulfur compounds like allicin, which have antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory effects.

items.title: Source of vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 supports protein metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from the bread and garlic helps maintain healthy blood hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Provides complex carbohydrates
items.content: The bread supplies slowly digestible carbs that provide sustained energy and satiety.

items.title: Includes healthy fats
items.content: Butter and occasional olive oil add monounsaturated fats that are beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The bread contains wheat, so people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should avoid it.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Butter and seasoning can raise the salt level, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Garlic bread is calorie‑rich; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Garlic allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to garlic, ranging from mild skin irritation to severe anaphylaxis.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Thaw the bread at room temperature or in the refrigerator, then bake in a preheated oven for 10‑15 minutes until golden. Serve hot as a standalone snack or alongside pasta, soups, and salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen garlic bread in the freezer at –18 °C. After thawing, consume within 2‑3 days and do not refreeze once fully defrosted.

content.title: About
content.content: The Whole Grain Muffin (2598) is a baked product made from whole grain flour, a small amount of sugar, and vegetable oil. It has a soft, slightly moist crumb and a gentle nutty aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain muffins retain most of the fiber and micronutrients of the grain.
The recipe often includes rolled oats, whole wheat, and whole rye.
Because whole grains are used, these muffins have a lower glycemic index than typical white muffins.
Traditionally they are served at breakfast with yogurt, fruit, or honey.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole grains provide both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs deliver sustained energy and promote satiety.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2 and B3 aid carbohydrate metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: The muffin supplies magnesium, iron and zinc, important for muscle and immune function.

items.title: Low in trans fats
items.content: When prepared with non‑hydrogenated vegetable oil, trans‑fat content remains minimal.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Contains wheat, so it is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although modest, the sugar should be accounted for by those monitoring blood glucose.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Whole grain muffins still provide calories, so portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the muffin as a snack, split it and spread cottage cheese, nut butter, or avocado. It pairs well with berries, honey, or low‑fat yogurt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer keeping, refrigerate up to 7 days or freeze in a zip‑lock bag.

content.title: About
content.content: PowerBar is a protein‑rich nutrition bar designed for athletes and active people. It provides fast‑digesting carbohydrates, protein, and a blend of vitamins to supply energy and support muscle recovery during and after workouts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: PowerBar was first launched in the early 1990s and quickly became a favorite among marathon runners.
The bars are available in a variety of flavors, including chocolate, nut, and fruit.
The formula often includes whey protein isolate, which is rapidly absorbed by the body.
Some PowerBar versions are fortified with creatine and BCAA for extra recovery benefits.
Bars are non‑crumbling and stay stable at moderate temperatures, making them easy to carry.

items.title: Quick energy replenishment
items.content: A mix of simple and complex carbs delivers an immediate glucose boost and sustains blood‑sugar levels during prolonged activity.

items.title: Supports muscle recovery
items.content: Whey protein helps repair muscle fibers after intense training sessions.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2, B6, and B12 aid energy metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Electrolyte content
items.content: Sodium and potassium help maintain fluid balance during sweating.

items.title: Convenient and portable
items.content: The bar is easy to store and transport, providing a practical nutrition source on the go.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Whey protein may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with dairy sensitivities.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Some PowerBar flavors contain significant amounts of sugar, which may be unsuitable for diabetics or those limiting sugar intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Bars are relatively calorie‑dense; they should be consumed in moderation, especially when managing weight.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Certain varieties use sucralose or aspartame, which some people prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Consume PowerBar 30‑60 minutes before exercise for energy or immediately after training for recovery. It can be paired with water, a sports drink, or blended into a protein shake.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, reseal the package tightly to prevent moisture absorption.

content.title: About
content.content: Thin‑crust cheese pizza is a popular fast‑food option made with a crisp, thin dough topped with tomato sauce and melted cheese. It is commonly served in quick‑serve restaurants and pizzerias.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thin crust cooks faster, allowing the pizza to be ready in 2‑3 minutes in a high‑heat oven.
The classic cheese used is mozzarella, but cheddar, parmesan, or a blend are often added.
In Italy, a similar thin pizza is called “pizza di marinara” or “Neapolitan,” though the traditional Neapolitan has a puffier edge.
Cheese pizza is a common vegetarian option because it contains no meat.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Cheese, especially mozzarella, is rich in calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Protein rich
items.content: Cheese provides high‑quality animal protein that supports tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 found in dairy supports nervous system function.

items.title: Lower carbohydrate content
items.content: Thin crust typically contains fewer carbs than a traditional thick crust, making it more suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Potential probiotics (when using fermented sauces)
items.content: Some tomato sauces are fermented, adding beneficial bacteria.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Cheese and sauce often contain a lot of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People who cannot digest lactose may experience discomfort from dairy ingredients.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein or whey can cause severe reactions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite the thin crust, cheese makes the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional dough contains gluten, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cheese pizza is usually eaten hot, sliced into wedges. Fresh herbs (basil, oregano) or a light drizzle of hot sauce can be added for extra flavor. For a lighter version, choose whole‑grain or gluten‑free crusts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore the crisp crust.

sausage-and-rice-with-mushroom-sauce.title: Sausage and Rice with Mushroom Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Sausage and rice with mushroom sauce is a ready‑to‑eat dish consisting of boiled rice, pieces of boiled or fried sausage, and a creamy mushroom sauce made from button mushrooms, cream and spices. It is served hot and works as a quick lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The mushroom sauce gives the dish a silky aroma and adds nutrients such as B‑vitamins and selenium.
Medium‑grain rice is usually used, keeping the grains separate and preventing a mushy texture when mixed.
The sausage can be pork, chicken or turkey, allowing the recipe to be adapted to different taste preferences.
The dish is common in cafeterias and casual restaurants as a "combo meal" because it balances protein, carbs and fats.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Sausage provides complete proteins needed for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Energy‑rich carbohydrates
items.content: Rice supplies complex carbs that release energy gradually, helping to keep you full longer.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Mushrooms are rich in B2, B3 and B5 vitamins, supporting metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Selenium and antioxidants
items.content: Mushrooms contain selenium and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: The creamy sauce adds modest amounts of calcium and phosphorus, important for bone health.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Processed sausages often contain a lot of salt, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: The cream sauce and fatty sausage increase saturated‑fat levels, a consideration for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Mushroom allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to mushrooms and should avoid this dish.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate (MSG)
items.content: Certain recipes add MSG as a flavor enhancer, which can cause sensitivity in some consumers.

content.title: How to Serve
content.content: Serve the dish hot, garnished with fresh herbs such as parsley or dill. A squeeze of lemon juice brightens the flavor, and a sprinkle of grated Parmesan adds extra richness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. When reheating, use a microwave or skillet and add a splash of water to prevent the sauce from drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Vegetable soup is a hot dish made from a variety of vegetables such as carrots, potatoes, onions, celery, and tomatoes simmered in broth. It has a gentle flavor, the aroma of fresh vegetables, and can be clear or creamy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegetable soups are traditional in many cultures, from French bouillon to Japanese miso soup.
Soups retain most vitamins and minerals because the vegetables are cooked in liquid rather than fried.
In some countries vegetable soup is considered a remedy for colds and flu.
Soups are easily adapted to vegan and gluten‑free diets.
When prepared correctly, vegetables keep a bright color, making the dish more appetizing.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: The vegetables provide vitamin C, vitamin A, folate and other micronutrients that support immunity.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: Because most of the volume is water, soup is suitable for weight management.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from the vegetables aids bowel function and promotes satiety.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: A warm broth helps replenish fluids, especially in cold weather.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Vegetable pigments such as carotenoids and lycopene have antioxidant effects.

items.title: Salt and sodium
items.content: Adding too much salt can increase sodium intake, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to certain vegetables, such as tomatoes or celery.

items.title: Contamination
items.content: If vegetables are not washed thoroughly, pesticides or bacteria may end up in the soup.

items.title: Nutrient loss
items.content: Overcooking vegetables can diminish their nutrient content and make them less beneficial.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve vegetable soup hot, often garnished with herbs, spices, or a drizzle of olive oil. It pairs well with whole‑grain bread or can be used as a side dish to a main course.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the soup to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 2‑3 months. Reheat to a rolling boil before serving.
